questions.stem: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Deforestation also increases atmospheric CO2. Why does cutting down forests have a double effect on CO2 levels?

options.text: Trees release CO2 when they are alive, so removing them stops this release
Fewer trees means less photosynthesis to remove CO2 from the air, AND burning or decomposing the cut trees releases the carbon stored in their biomass as CO2
Deforestation increases rainfall, which dissolves more CO2
Deforestation only affects local CO2 levels, not global levels

questions.explanation: Deforestation has two effects on CO2: (1) it removes trees that were absorbing CO2 through photosynthesis, reducing the rate of CO2 removal from the atmosphere, and (2) when the felled trees are burned or decompose, the carbon stored in their biomass is released back as CO2. This is why deforestation is a significant contributor to rising atmospheric CO2 levels.

questions.stem: In the carbon cycle, carbon moves from the atmosphere into living organisms and back. Which process removes carbon dioxide from the atmosphere?

options.text: Respiration
Combustion
Photosynthesis
Decomposition

questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the only major biological process that removes CO2 from the atmosphere, converting it into glucose (organic carbon compounds). Respiration, combustion, and decomposition all release CO2 back into the atmosphere. This is why plants and algae are sometimes called 'carbon sinks' - they store carbon that was previously in the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Millions of years ago, dead organisms were buried and compressed to form fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas). A student says this carbon was 'removed from the carbon cycle.' Why is this not entirely accurate?

options.text: The carbon was destroyed when the organisms died
The carbon was locked away for a very long time but is now being rapidly returned to the cycle through human combustion of fossil fuels
Fossil fuels do not contain carbon
The carbon cycle did not exist millions of years ago

questions.explanation: Carbon in fossil fuels was effectively removed from the active carbon cycle for millions of years - stored underground as a carbon reservoir. However, humans burning fossil fuels are now releasing this ancient carbon back into the atmosphere as CO2 much faster than natural processes can absorb it. The carbon was not permanently removed; it was just stored for a long time.

questions.stem: Decomposers play a vital role in the carbon cycle. If all decomposers were removed from an ecosystem, what would happen to carbon cycling?

options.text: Carbon cycling would speed up because organisms would decompose faster
Dead organisms and waste would accumulate, locking up carbon in organic matter and preventing it from being recycled back to the atmosphere and soil
Nothing would change because decomposers are not important in the carbon cycle
Plants would absorb more CO2 to compensate

questions.explanation: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organisms and waste products, returning carbon to the atmosphere as CO2 through respiration and to the soil as mineral ions. Without decomposers, dead organic matter would accumulate, and the carbon locked within it would not be recycled. Eventually, the supply of CO2 for photosynthesis and minerals for plant growth would be depleted.

questions.stem: The oceans absorb about 25% of the CO2 released by human activities. Some of this CO2 dissolves in seawater and forms carbonic acid, lowering the ocean's pH. What is the potential ecological impact of this ocean acidification?

options.text: Fish grow larger in acidic water
Organisms with calcium carbonate shells or skeletons (like corals and shellfish) struggle to build and maintain their structures in more acidic water
Ocean acidification increases photosynthesis by marine plants
Acidic oceans evaporate faster, reducing sea levels

questions.explanation: When CO2 dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid, lowering the pH (ocean acidification). More acidic conditions make it harder for organisms like corals, molluscs, and some plankton to form their calcium carbonate shells and skeletons - the acid can even dissolve existing structures. Since coral reefs support about 25% of marine species, this has huge implications for ocean biodiversity.
